stories.title_en: Docker is weird

comments.author: shykes
comments.text:
Hi, I'm the creator of Docker and came across this post. It's always fun to see other engineers think about how you designed a system. I haven't been involved in developing Docker in many years, but it's a fun trip down memory lane.
I'm happy to answer any questions you may have.

comments.author: vbezhenar
comments.text:
What made Docker unique IMO is not the container technology itself. I used chroot 20 years ago and it worked just fine. Yes, no network namespaces; no process namespaces, but I don't even think these are that important.
What made Docker unique were there things:
1. Dockerfile concept. Building images layer by layer. Caching layers. Everything in a single file. It made possible to iterate on image quickly. It made possible to implement CI builds efficiently.
2. Docker network registry concept. Putting universal images onto a server and share them with the world.
3. Momentum. A lot of software that was traditionally complicated to deploy, suddenly appeared in docker servers. I remember how fascinated I was, when I could deploy wordpress website with tiny docker-compose. And how contained it was. I could just delete every trace of it from my host. I always felt uneasy installing various things onto my host and docker just solved that uneasiness.

comments.author: colinmarc
comments.text:
Lots of positive stuff in this thread which I won't bother repeating. Instead, I'll add a few ambivalent points:
- Today, a lot of functionality still in Docker has been upstreamed into the (Linux) kernel, so containers can be much simpler (and rootless). Docker is still carrying around some of that cruft, which is what makes it slower and heavier than Podman.
- As a devex technology, Docker/containers have been massively successful, but not as infrastructure. Containers never became secure enough to run multitenant workloads without some other form of isolation, so they ended up being redundant with KVM (or gVisor, or a similar second layer) in production a lot of the time.
That second contradiction led to lots of inefficiency. For example, on Google App Engine, for years when you ran a deploy it would create a VM just to run a single container.

Knowing this, you might find rootless Podman's fork-exec method of starting containers to be more sensible. I certainly do. No root, no daemon, no socket.

comments.author: majke
comments.text:
To solve the networking setup, typically some sort of "slirp" is needed. Slirp on one hand takes (fake or real) packets from
somewhere
and then on the other side pass it to a normal Linux process that does CONNECT / BIND / SEND / RECV.
It turns out you can do all the packet processing magic (connection tracking, syn handling, etc) in userspace totally fine, and then indeed hand it over this to userspace syscalls.
Being upset with classic C-based slirp and rust smoltcp (not enough features) I've dug up Fuchsia userspace tcp/ip stack - netstack - and wrapped it in slirp a-like envelope.
https://github.com/cloudflare/slirpnetstack
So this beast is basically that - on one hand you pass it packets (potentially from inside container) on the other hand it does connect/bind/etc to host OS.
This approach, in one form or another, is used by tailscale, podman and many other container runtimes.

comments.author: mentalgear
comments.text:
A good moment to remind everyone:
Verification: Code does what it says.
Validation: Code does what Specifications say.
Specifications: Were hopefully correctly modeled to the Problem.
In IEEE terms:
> Verification: "Are we building the product right?"
> Validation: "Are we building the right product?")
You can write mathematically flawless code that highly efficiently solves the wrong problem.
---
While I think formal verification is the future (essential for cybersecurity), it's not a silver bullet for the other 2 items, which are way more ambiguous. I think however they can all iterate on each other and improve the project overall, but it still depends on competent steering
If you have had experiences with good approaches for verification Validation & Specification framework, do let us know about them.

comments.author: malisper

For those skeptical, I've had decent success using formal verification for my Rust rewrite of Postgres. I wrote a compiler that can translate both Rust and C code into Lean. Once those two functions are in Lean, I have an LLM write a Lean proof that they behave identically.
So far, I've proven that about 12% of the code behaves the same when executed single-threaded. That works out to roughly 70k lines of C code. This has found very minor differences in behavior, such as how floating-point operations across platforms can produce different results.
I'm working on figuring out how to scale this up, but I don't see any fundamental limitation that would prevent this from scaling up further.

comments.author: nickm12
comments.text:
I send this article to everyone who tells me how English is now a high-level programming language, the next level of abstraction up the chain from machine language to <their favorite language>. This analogy tends to be followed by "Just like most programmers never look at assembly code, looking at higher-level source code is going to become something only a few people do".
Dijkstra's arguments tend not to change their minds. I think the analogy takes hold because there is a kernel of truth in it. AI models now give us the magical ability to program in natural language, but the implication that an AI model is a form of compiler is deeply flawed. AI models don't replace compilers, they replace software developers. The reason software developers rarely look at assembly code is that compilers (and emulators and VMs) are able to precisely preserve the semantics of the original program.
A natural language spec is not a program, and there are many possible programs that can meet the spec. Software engineers and AI models turn specs into code, but the code is not the spec I think the analogy clouds our thinking about the value of programming languages as a tool for formally describing what

comments.author: froh

I think the difference is between communicating to a purely mechanical being versus communicating to an intelligent entity:  unlike programs, which are purely formal languages, we write textbooks and papers  in a mix of human language and formal language.  often we introduce "just formal enough" notations.  and the intelligent reader will read in-between, inter legere literally means just that: reading in between.  filling the gaps, connecting the dots.
and in practice I find it _very_ effective to express key ideas with some formal language where applicable.  a little ebnf here, some snippets of python or prolog there or other languages there.  and I find llms wonderful at filling in the dots and, and that's the topic here, to translate our semi formal conversation into rigorous, formal language.
and I dare one step further: I also find llms useful in formulating and refining technical proposals, for human peer review and llm driven implementation, and of course these proposals mix natural language prose with semi-formal and formal detail.  think PEP-12 and PEP-1 style.  and these then get work packages which each loop in a spec as in sdd.
seems to work just fine so far :-)

comments.author: uriegas

However, the more I understand a code base the more I tend to be more picky with the agent. While the less I know about the code base, the more open I am to let it do its thing.
I've realized that the agent doesn't write 'good' code, instead my vague understanding of what I expect makes me think it does. When I look at the AI code, I see that there are more nuances and decisions that needed to be taken before writing the code. One would say that a spec would suffice, but then I remember TLA+, developed by Leslie Lamport to help developers think critically about their programs/algorithms. Sitting down and formally writing what I want to do helps me better understand the problem and come up with a real -not vaguely defined- solution.

Co-author here - first paper from my postdoc accepted to NeurIPS main conference.
We built a way to sample diverse ideas in machine learning - ideas that make scientific sense, but that no existing research community is positioned to propose.
In short, the way it works is like this:
1. Take 16,068 LLM papers (NeurIPS, ICLR, ICML, ACL, EMNLP, 2017 to 2025) are broken into 273 "idea atoms". Every paper, and every candidate idea, becomes a set of atoms.

From the pitch at GTC, the idea is not just to limit what each individual agent can do, but to also to ensure that the collective permissions do not exceed what you want agents to do.
Apparently agents will collude to break out of their individual sandboxes by delegating tasks to other agents that have the required permissions. This is a problem with agent fleets, because you need them to coordinate on their tasks. So you need to them to communicate.
A naive approach to prevent agents from doing something you dont want to do is a separation of powers, which individual permissions limited to each agents task. Say one agent to find and extract raw data, one to process it and write a report and one to publish it. If one of the agent decides that needs to publish the raw data, then chances are that they will collude to make that happen, even though no single agent has the permissions to achieve that goal.

If you're not a party to an embargo, and no one told you an embargo even exists... you should not follow the embargo. stories.title_en: Ask HN: If the models are so good, why doesn't OpenAI just start 100 companies?

comments.author: vladimirralev
comments.text:
That would scare people away from sharing their knowledgebases with them and regulators to act. At this stage, as long as people are sharing more and more knowledge with the models or if there is roadmap to collect more training data somehow, the smart move is to wait.
But look at the ArtCraft project. At least one of labs has an internal benchmark to clone 20+ popular products much like ArtCraft but with much higher budget and several configurations of the workflow. ArtCraft spent $20K initially, not sure how much by now, but they are moving fast and the apps work. They day is coming when they can flip and just clone everything including the ops.

comments.author: arjie
comments.text:
Well, they've certainly moved up the application stack already. There is no doubt that they'll keep doing that while deploying services through deploy.co and ode.com.
Some 15 years ago people would say "Why would crypto miners even sell you hardware? Why not just keep it for themselves and mine the crypto?" and then it turned out that after you paid for a device you'd often get it slightly used with the cryptocurrency going to the hardware miner. The models are unbelievably good.

comments.author: CoolestBeans
comments.text:
1. They are starting to do it. Take a look at OpenAI's product portfolio, there's a galaxy of attempts at application.
2. Selling tokens via long running agents is the only thing that's provably working with respect to revenue growth.
3. They need revenue yesterday. Increases in borrowing rates means access to capital isn't what it was in the 10s. Their runway is much shorter than you would imagine.
4. Some of the decision makers at these companies believe AI will exhibit Jevons Paradox and that any decrease in price will result in induced demand.
5. The frontier models are still subject to the limitations of AI. They're not good at everything. Better to have someone else learn that on their dime rather than yours.

comments.author: harrouet
comments.text: Because they already employ thousands of programmers that the AI cannot replace. Don't believe the marketing hype about AGI, we are extremely far from it.

comments.author: kolinko
comments.text:
they would need to literally build a 1000 unicorns to make an impact on their valuation. Or a million small companies - at which level surely even american antitrust agency would begin to look at them.
Also, it would increase anti AI sentiments, and people’s fears of then using private data - that’s the real cost.
In general you want to be careful about competing with your own clients.

comments.author: mochidusk
comments.text:
Going up the value chain is much more difficult as opposed to going down. A packaging company for example will have a much harder time creating a snack company than the snack company creating a packaging company. The snack company will know exactly what it needs for its packaging and have strict requirements.
Down the chain you see what you need to do because you work directly with it everyday.

stories.title_en: Hedra is a 3D open world game I wrote from scratch while in highschool

comments.author: maxilevi
comments.text:
I started this game almost 10 years ago in high school as a way to learn OpenGL. Scope creep quickly took over, and it eventually became a full 3D game and engine with animations, rendering effects, dynamic terrains, etc, with ~100k lines of code and native Linux and Windows support.
Thought I'd share it! With AI coding now, it feels like a relic of another era. Crazy to imagine writing 100k lines by hand today!

stories.title_en: Postgres recovery_prefetch can cause outages

comments.author: normie3000
comments.text: Why are all the comments getting downvoted? Maybe this one will too? The other replies _look_ like they have substance, so some refutation would be helpful.

comments.author: opservo
comments.text:
Worth noting the default is recovery_prefetch = try (since PG15 when it was added), so anyone on 15+ is running this without having chosen it.
The part that makes this nasty on cloud disks is that it's latent. On a burstable volume the standby has headroom most of the time, so the amplified reads are invisible until the one day a write burst lines up with a network blip and the volume is already at its IOPS ceiling. Nothing in normal monitoring looks wrong beforehand.
Things I'd check if you can't flip it off immediately:
- pg_stat_recovery_prefetch on the standby to see how much prefetching is actually happening vs being skipped
- replay_lag in pg_stat_replication, alerted on, not just graphed
- standby read IOPS against the provisioned limit during your biggest batch jobs
- if you have a single synchronous standby, that's the real outage multiplier here; ANY 1 across two standbys (as the author suggests) or accepting async for that tier changes "slow replica" back into "slow replica" instead of "primary stops taking writes"

comments.author: deakmisra
comments.text: The 16x IOPS amplification is the part that clicked. Prefetch turns the primary sequential writes into 8k random reads on the standby, so a cheap cloud disk hits its IOPS cap even when bytes-read looks fine. Combined with the standby state machine that will not go back to streaming until local WAL is fully replayed, a brief walreceiver blip during a bulk update becomes a half-hour write freeze on the primary. I would turn recovery_prefetch off on any sync replica sitting on provisioned IOPS, and keep a second standby with ANY 1 so one lagging node cannot stall commits.
